title: Surdas
hook: a small boy with butter on his face makes his case

segments.voice: Yesterday: Surdas turned from his own sorrow to a little boy asking when his braid would grow. Look down, like a mother.

The complaint comes from the neighbors. Butter is missing from their houses again. Pots are cracked. There are small handprints. So the accused is brought before his mother, and the song lets us see his face, still shiny with butter. He doesn't cry or run. He opens his mouth and begins his defense. It's one of the songs carried under the name of Surdas, and it plays like a tiny courtroom: one small boy, no lawyer, and an argument he has clearly been working on.
screen: `THE NEIGHBORS COMPLAIN.` → `BUTTER ON HIS FACE.` → `THE DEFENSE BEGINS.`

segments.voice: It opens with the line the whole song hangs on. Maiya mori, main nahin makhan khayo. Mother, I didn't eat the butter. Then the case, point by point. One: at dawn you sent me off behind the cows, and I wandered the forest all day. When would I have had time? Two: look at these arms. I'm a child. How could I reach a pot hung up high? Three: the cowherd boys have it in for me. They smeared it on my face themselves. Then he changes tactics and gets hurt. Mother, you're too trusting, you believe whatever they say. Maybe you think I'm somebody else's child. And the big finish: here, take back my stick and my blanket. I quit. You've made me dance enough. The song ends: Surdas says, then Yashoda smiled, and pulled him close against her heart. Case closed. The butter never comes up again. The Bhagavata told how the butter thief stole. Surdas adds the defense, and gives the last word to a mother's smile. Her love doesn't wait for the verdict, or need him to be innocent. And the singer writes his own name into the last line, standing in the yard as a witness, watching Yashoda laugh. For a singer the tradition remembers as blind, it's a striking place to stand: the one who sees the scolding turn into a hug.
screen: `MOTHER, I DIDN'T EAT THE BUTTER.` · `DAWN, SMALL ARMS, JEALOUS FRIENDS.` · `TAKE BACK MY STICK. I QUIT.` · then, large: `YASHODA SMILED AND PULLED HIM CLOSE.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind someone who gets things wrong around you and argues their way out: a child, a coworker, maybe you. Hear the defense the way Yashoda hears it, every point lined up, a little dramatic, and instead of ruling on it, picture smiling and opening your arms. You don't have to agree with the argument; just let the warmth arrive first, and if you pray, bring that person into your prayer.
Surdas. The singer who let a small boy argue his case, and gave the last line to his mother's smile.
Your line: warmth before the verdict. A mother's smile settled the whole case. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: Maiya mori, main nahin makhan khayo is sung as a bhajan in homes and temples, and around Krishna's birthday, Janmashtami, children sometimes act out the butter thief's story.

Yes, she makes him give his stick and blanket to the neighbors for good.

chat.meaning: The song ends with Surdas watching Yashoda smile and hold him close. The butter never comes up again.

Maiya.meaning: mother, the way a child says it

Yashoda.meaning: Krishna's foster mother in the cowherd village

Bhagavata.meaning: the Bhagavata Purana, which tells Krishna's childhood

Surdas.meaning: the singer of Braj, remembered as blind
